line: # Plate summary (as read from mavor1792_alphabet_plateI.jpg only):
# Vowels a, e, i are rendered as a small comma/apostrophe mark; o, u, y as a small dot. In isolation these six marks
# look alike; the plate's separate "Vowel Places" table says the vowel is distinguished by WHERE the dot/comma sits
# relative to a consonant's own character (a set of six positions, one column per vowel, shown for each consonant
# row b,d,f,g,h,k,l,m,n,p,q,s,l,v,w,x). Consonants: b = small hook open left ("c"-like); d = the mirror hook open
# right; c = a short tick with a small curling tail (also used, unlabelled, as the z abbrev-column filler, so c and
# z are not visually distinguished on this plate); f = a hook with a small loop; g/j = a loop with a descending
# tail; h = a short upward tick; k = a plain backslash diagonal; l = a plain forward-slash diagonal; m = a wide
# arc opening downward (cap shape); n = a narrower arc opening upward (cup shape); p = a hook with a loop near the
# top; q = a rounded loop like a cursive e; r = a short curved tick similar to h; s = a short horizontal dash; t =
# a short vertical bar; v = a loop with a descending tail (similar to g/j); w = a short horizontal dash/hook; x = a
# small loop with a short tail; z = a squiggle, drawn the same as the c abbrev filler. Double/triple consonants:
# ch = a small hooked tick; sh = a "6"-shaped loop; th = a small tick similar to ch; thr = a looped tick with a
# small tail; str = a "9"-shaped loop; wh = a plain short dash, drawn the same as s.
# Confidence: LOW. The strip images are narrow, low-resolution photographs of fine 18th-century copperplate
# engraving with no magnification available; several plate letters share near-identical stroke families (b/d,
# m/n, p/f/g/v, c/z, s/wh) that are only distinguished in the source by small differences in curvature and closure
# this reader could not reliably resolve, and the vowel marks could not be matched to the Vowel Places table with
# confidence in most words. Roughly half of the signs in each line are marked "?" for this reason; letters given
# without "?" are the shapes closest to an unambiguous plate match, not confirmed readings.
